name: Batting average
seoDesc: Batting average: work out number of times out from the runs scored and the batting average. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: Supply the runs scored, the batting average, number of hits and number of official at-bats and the Batting average calculator solves for number of times out. It suits a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Batting average calculator work?
sections.html:
The Batting average calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of times out in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (choose the sport); then you type in the runs scored, the batting average (Cricket batting average), number of hits and number of official at-bats.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Batting average calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Number of times out=runs scored ÷ batting average
Batting average=number of hits ÷ number of official at-bats

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.html:

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Number of times out = 1 should be roughly the size you expected from Choose the sport set to Cricket and Runs scored = 10.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Batting average calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the runs scored, the batting average and number of hits — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Batting average calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of times out, derived from the runs scored, the batting average and number of hits. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Batting average calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the runs scored, the batting average, number of hits and number of official at-bats, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Number of times out = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Batting average calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
